edits.text:
# SlipI-OS

A browser-based desktop environment inspired by DaedalOS. SlipI OS is intended to use CheerpX for its Linux runtime, with browser-persistent storage built on IndexedDB and ZenFS.

## Development

```sh
npm install
npm run dev
```

The current desktop shell is an initial UI foundation. The terminal surface is not connected to a Linux runtime yet; CheerpX integration, persistent filesystem setup, and application services are planned next.

# SlipI-OS
its a web os, based on daedalos, but will use CheerpX as the Linux engine rather than slow v86

## Browser Application API

Applications are independent HTML files with assets referenced relative to their own HTML file. The desktop loads each app in an iframe. Launch flags are query parameters, so they do not change relative asset resolution:

```text
Applications/example/index.html?--is_windowed&--window_size=640x720
```

Use the desktop's Open app button or call `window.WebOS.openApp(url, options)`. App options support `title`, `icon`, `isWindowed`, `windowSize`, `width`, and `height`. The host also exposes `openWindow`, `getWindows`, `closeWindow`, `minimizeWindow`, `maximizeWindow`, and `resizeWindow`.

An app under `WebOS filesystem/Applications/<app>/` can load `../../app-api.js`. It exposes `window.WebOSApp.flags` (`isWindowed`, `windowSize`, and `windowId`) and `openApp`, `close`, `minimize`, `maximize`, `resize`, `setTitle`, and `setIcon`. App-to-host requests use `postMessage` and are accepted only from registered app iframes.

The API example is at `WebOS filesystem/Applications/api-example/index.html`. The Nuvola icon theme is extracted to `WebOS filesystem/Icons/nuvola/`; attribution and license notices are included with the theme.

:root { font-family: Tahoma, Arial, sans-serif; color: #111; background: #c0c0c0; }
.desktop { position: relative; width: 100%; height: 100dvh; min-height: 320px; overflow: hidden; background: #c0c0c0; }
.workspace { position: absolute; inset: 0 0 34px; overflow: hidden; background: #c0c0c0; }

.window { position: absolute; display: flex; flex-direction: column; min-width: min(260px, 100%); min-height: 210px; overflow: hidden; border: 2px solid; border-color: #fff #404040 #404040 #fff; outline: 1px solid #111; background: linear-gradient(180deg, #dedede 0%, #bdbdbd 100%); box-shadow: 1px 1px 0 #808080 inset; }

.window-titlebar { flex: 0 0 27px; display: flex; align-items: center; padding: 0 0 0 6px; color: #111; background: linear-gradient(180deg, #e2e2e2 0%, #c1c1c1 54%, #aaa 100%); touch-action: none; user-select: none; cursor: grab; }
.window-title { overflow: hidden; font-size: 12px; font-weight: 700; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap; }
.window-controls { align-self: stretch; display: flex; gap: 0; margin-left: auto; }

.window-controls button { position: relative; display: grid; align-self: stretch; width: 24px; height: auto; place-items: center; padding: 0; border: 0; border-left: 1px solid #888; border-right: 1px solid #eee; border-bottom: 1px solid #666; color: #111; background: linear-gradient(180deg, #eee 0%, #c5c5c5 58%, #aaa 100%); cursor: pointer; }
.window-controls button:active { border-left-color: #555; border-right-color: #ddd; border-bottom-color: #444; filter: brightness(.92); }
.control-icon { position: relative; display: block; width: 12px; height: 12px; }
.icon-minimize::after { position: absolute; top: 7px; left: 1px; width: 10px; border-top: 2px solid currentColor; content: ""; }
.icon-close::before, .icon-close::after { position: absolute; top: 5px; left: 1px; width: 11px; border-top: 2px solid currentColor; content: ""; transform: rotate(45deg); }
.window-content { flex: 1; min-height: 0; margin: 2px; border: 1px solid; border-color: #777 #fff #fff #777; background: linear-gradient(180deg, #e2e2e2 0%, #c8c8c8 100%); }
.resize-handle { position: absolute; right: 1px; bottom: 1px; width: 13px; height: 13px; cursor: nwse-resize; touch-action: none; }
.resize-handle::after { position: absolute; right: 2px; bottom: 2px; width: 7px; height: 7px; border-right: 1px solid #404040; border-bottom: 1px solid #404040; content: ""; }
.taskbar { position: absolute; z-index: 20; inset: auto 0 0; height: 34px; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 4px; padding: 3px; border-top: 1px solid #fff; background: #c0c0c0; }

.new-window, .taskbar-window { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 5px; height: 27px; padding: 0 7px; border: 1px solid; border-color: #fff #404040 #404040 #fff; color: #111; background: #c0c0c0; font-size: 11px; cursor: pointer; }
.window-list { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 4px; min-width: 0; overflow-x: auto; }
.taskbar-window span:last-child { overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap; }
.taskbar-window-icon { position: relative; flex: 0 0 14px; width: 14px; height: 12px; border: 1px solid currentColor; }
.taskbar-window-icon::after { position: absolute; top: 3px; left: 0; right: 0; border-top: 1px solid currentColor; content: ""; }

# Curated Nuvola Icons

This extracted theme is the runtime subset for SlipI OS. The original archive remains beside this folder as the untouched source.

## Sizes

- `16x16`: taskbar, compact controls, and tray
- `22x22`: menus, toolbar controls, and tray
- `32x32`: file manager rows, app launchers, and category views
- `48x48`: desktop icons and larger built-in app launchers

## Complete Categories

The following categories are kept at all four sizes:

- `places`: desktop/home/trash locations, regular and open folders, folder colors, and named folders
- `mimetypes`: file and document types
- `status`: notification and system-tray states
- `devices`: drives, removable storage, and connected devices
- `categories`: filesystem and application categories

## Selected Actions

The `actions` directories keep application-menu/exit, document open/new/save/close/print, copy/cut/paste, folder creation, navigation, search, refresh, window open/close, and help icons.

## Selected Built-In Apps

The `apps` directories keep icons for the file manager, browser, terminal, text editor, calculator, system settings, application/package management, system monitor, font viewer, search, calendar, and generic window/application entries.

Theme attribution and licensing remain in `CREDITS.md`, `author.txt`, `license.txt`, and `readme.txt`; the archive itself is preserved separately.

terminalCommandOutput.text:
--- @zenfs/core ---
# ZenFS

ZenFS is a cross-platform library that emulates the [Node.js filesystem API](http://nodejs.org/api/fs.html).
It works using a system of backends, which are used by ZenFS to store and retrieve data.
ZenFS should cover the full API surface of the latest Node.js version, though complex changes may lag a little bit.

## Backends

ZenFS is modular and easily extended. The core includes some built-in backends:

- `InMemory`: Stores files in-memory. This is cleared when the runtime ends (e.g. a user navigating away from a web page or a Node process exiting)
- `CopyOnWrite`: Use readable and writable file systems with [copy-on-write](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copy-on-write).
- `Fetch`: Downloads files over HTTP with the `fetch` API
- `Port`: Interacts with a remote over a `MessagePort`-like interface (e.g. a worker)
- `Passthrough`: Use an existing `node:fs` interface with ZenFS
- `SingleBuffer`: A backend contained within a single buffer. Can be used for synchronous multi-threaded operations using `SharedArrayBuffer`

ZenFS supports a number of other backends.
Many are provided as separate packages under `@zenfs`.
More backends can be defined by separate libraries by extending the `FileSystem` class and providing a `Backend` object.

You can find all of the packages available over on [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/org/zenfs). Below is a list of the backends included with some of them:

- @zenfs/archives: `Zip`, `Iso`
- @zenfs/cloud: `Dropbox`, `GoogleDrive`, `S3Bucket`
- @zenfs/dom: `WebAccess` (Web [File System Access API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/File_System_API)/OPFS), `IndexedDB`, `WebStorage` (`localStorage`/`sessionStorage`), `XML` (DOM elements)
- @zenfs/emscripten: `Emscripten` and a plugin for Emscripten's file system API

As an added bonus, all ZenFS backends support synchronous operations.
Additionally, all of the backends included with the core are cross-platform.

For more information, see the [docs](https://zenfs.dev/core).

## Installing

```sh
npm install @zenfs/core
```

If you're using ZenFS, especially for big projects, please consider supporting the project.
Thousands of hours have been dedicated to its development.
Your financial support would go a long way toward improving ZenFS and its community.

## Usage

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **[Check out the ZenFS docs!](https://zenfs.dev/start/usage/)**

```js
import { fs } from '@zenfs/core'; // You can also use the default export

fs.writeFileSync('/test.txt', 'You can do this anywhere, including browsers!');

const contents = fs.readFileSync('/test.txt', 'utf-8');
console.log(contents);
```

A single `InMemory` backend is created by default, mounted on `/`. To use different backends, and to
mount more than one, configure ZenFS with `configure`. This mounts a zip file to `/mnt/zip`,
in-memory storage to `/tmp`, and IndexedDB to `/home`:

```js
import { configure, InMemory } from '@zenfs/core';
import { IndexedDB } from '@zenfs/dom';
import { Zip } from '@zenfs/archives';

const res = await fetch('mydata.zip');

await configure({
[8Cmounts: {
[16C'/mnt/zip': { backend: Zip, data: await res.arrayBuffer() },
[16C'/tmp': InMemory,
[16C'/home': IndexedDB,
[8C},
});
```

# ZenFS DOM Backends

[ZenFS](https://github.com/zen-fs/core) backends for DOM APIs. DOM APIs are _only_ available natively in browsers.

Please read the ZenFS core documentation!

## Backends

- `WebStorage` stores files in a `Storage` object, like `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`.
- `IndexedDB` stores files into an `IndexedDB` object database.
- `WebAccess` uses the [File System Access API](https://developer.mozilla.org/Web/API/File_System_API).
- `XML` uses an `XMLDocument` to store files, which can be appended to the DOM.

For more information, see the [API documentation](https://zenfs.dev/dom/).

## Usage

You can use the backends from `@zenfs/dom` just like the backends from `@zenfs/core`:

```js
import { configure, fs } from '@zenfs/core';
import { WebStorage } from '@zenfs/dom';

await configureSingle({ backend: WebStorage, storage: localStorage });

if (!fs.existsSync('/test.txt')) {
[8Cfs.writeFileSync('/test.txt', 'This will persist across reloads!');
}

const contents = fs.readFileSync('/test.txt', 'utf-8');
console.log(contents);
```

#### `XML`

The `XML` backend can be used to create a file system which lives in the DOM:

```html
<!-- ... -->
<fs />
<!-- ... -->
```

```js
import { configure, fs } from '@zenfs/core';
import { XML } from '@zenfs/dom';

await configureSingle({
[8Cbackend: XML,
[8Croot: document.querySelector('fs'), // root is optional
});

fs.writeFileSync('/test.txt', 'This is in the DOM!');
```

If you choose to add the root element to the DOM by appending it, you will likely want to hide its contents (`display:none` works well).

The `root` option is not required. If you choose not to pass in a `root`, you can always append it to the DOM later:

```js
import { configure, fs, mounts } from '@zenfs/core';
import { XML } from '@zenfs/dom';

await configureSingle({ backend: XML });

const { root } = mounts.get('/');

document.body.append(root);
```

This may disrupt use cases that involve saving the HTML file locally and loading it later, since a new element is created when configuring. In contrast, when using an existing element and passing in a `root`, the existing element's contents will be preserved.[?2004h

# SlipI-OS
its a web os, based on daedalos, but will use CheerpX as the Linux engine rather than slow v86

## Browser Application API

Applications are independent HTML files with assets referenced relative to their own HTML file. The desktop loads each app in an iframe. Launch flags are query parameters, so they do not change relative asset resolution:

```text
Applications/example/index.html?--is_windowed&--window_size=640x720
```

Use the desktop's Open app button or call `window.WebOS.openApp(url, options)`. App options support `title`, `icon`, `isWindowed`, `windowSize`, `width`, and `height`. The host also exposes `openWindow`, `getWindows`, `closeWindow`, `minimizeWindow`, `maximizeWindow`, and `resizeWindow`.

An app under `WebOS filesystem/Applications/<app>/` can load `../../app-api.js`. --- @zenfs/core ---
# ZenFS

ZenFS is a cross-platform library that emulates the [Node.js filesystem API](htt
p://nodejs.org/api/fs.html).
It works using a system of backends, which are used by ZenFS to store and retrie
ve data.
ZenFS should cover the full API surface of the latest Node.js version, though co
mplex changes may lag a little bit.

## Backends

ZenFS is modular and easily extended. The core includes some built-in backends:

- `InMemory`: Stores files in-memory. This is cleared when the runtime ends (e.g
. a user navigating away from a web page or a Node process exiting)
- `CopyOnWrite`: Use readable and writable file systems with [copy-on-write](htt
ps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copy-on-write).
- `Fetch`: Downloads files over HTTP with the `fetch` API
- `Port`: Interacts with a remote over a `MessagePort`-like interface (e.g. a wo
rker)
- `Passthrough`: Use an existing `node:fs` interface with ZenFS
- `SingleBuffer`: A backend contained within a single buffer. Can be used for sy
nchronous multi-threaded operations using `SharedArrayBuffer`

ZenFS supports a number of other backends.
Many are provided as separate packages under `@zenfs`.
More backends can be defined by separate libraries by extending the `FileSystem`
 class and providing a `Backend` object.

You can find all of the packages available over on [NPM](https://www.npmjs.com/o
rg/zenfs). Below is a list of the backends included with some of them:

- @zenfs/archives: `Zip`, `Iso`
- @zenfs/cloud: `Dropbox`, `GoogleDrive`, `S3Bucket`
- @zenfs/dom: `WebAccess` (Web [File System Access API](https://developer.mozill
a.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/File_System_API)/OPFS), `IndexedDB`, `WebStorage` (`loc
alStorage`/`sessionStorage`), `XML` (DOM elements)
- @zenfs/emscripten: `Emscripten` and a plugin for Emscripten's file system API

As an added bonus, all ZenFS backends support synchronous operations.
Additionally, all of the backends included with the core are cross-platform.

For more information, see the [docs](https://zenfs.dev/core).

## Installing

```sh
npm install @zenfs/core
```

If you're using ZenFS, especially for big projects, please consider supporting t
he project.
Thousands of hours have been dedicated to its development.
Your financial support would go a long way toward improving ZenFS and its commun
ity.

## Usage

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **[Check out the ZenFS docs!](https://zenfs.dev/start/usage/)**

```js
import { fs } from '@zenfs/core'; // You can also use the default export

fs.writeFileSync('/test.txt', 'You can do this anywhere, including browsers!');

const contents = fs.readFileSync('/test.txt', 'utf-8');
console.log(contents);
```

A single `InMemory` backend is created by default, mounted on `/`. To use differ
ent backends, and to
mount more than one, configure ZenFS with `configure`. This mounts a zip file to
 `/mnt/zip`,
in-memory storage to `/tmp`, and IndexedDB to `/home`:

```js
import { configure, InMemory } from '@zenfs/core';
import { IndexedDB } from '@zenfs/dom';
import { Zip } from '@zenfs/archives';

const res = await fetch('mydata.zip');

await configure({
        mounts: {
                '/mnt/zip': { backend: Zip, data: await res.arrayBuffer() },
                '/tmp': InMemory,
                '/home': IndexedDB,
        },
});
```

The `fs/promises` API is available from `@zenfs/core/promises`, as the `promises
` export, or as
`fs.promises`.

For the full usage guide, see **[the documentation](https://zenfs.dev/start/usag
e/)**.
This includes mounting at runtime, contexts and permissions, devices, and the `n
ode:*`module emulation.

## Bundling

ZenFS exports a drop-in for Node's `fs` module, so you can use it for your bundl
er of preference using the default export.
See [COPYING.md](./COPYING.md) for more info.

## Sponsors

A huge thank you to [deco.cx](https://github.com/deco-cx) for sponsoring ZenFS a
nd helping to make this possible.

## Contact and Support

You can reach out [on Discord](https://zenfs.dev/discord) or by emailing jp@zenf
s.dev

## License

[ZenFS](https://github.com/zen-fs/core) is licensed under the [LGPL 3.0 or later
](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.html) and [COPYING.md](https://github.co
m/zen-fs/core/blob/main/COPYING.md).
Copyright © James Prevett and other ZenFS contributors.

# ZenFS DOM Backends

[ZenFS](https://github.com/zen-fs/core) backends for DOM APIs. DOM APIs are _onl
y_ available natively in browsers.

Please read the ZenFS core documentation!

## Backends

- `WebStorage` stores files in a `Storage` object, like `localStorage` and `sess
ionStorage`.
- `IndexedDB` stores files into an `IndexedDB` object database.
- `WebAccess` uses the [File System Access API](https://developer.mozilla.org/We
b/API/File_System_API).
- `XML` uses an `XMLDocument` to store files, which can be appended to the DOM.

For more information, see the [API documentation](https://zenfs.dev/dom/).

## Usage

You can use the backends from `@zenfs/dom` just like the backends from `@zenfs/c
ore`:

```js
import { configure, fs } from '@zenfs/core';
import { WebStorage } from '@zenfs/dom';

await configureSingle({ backend: WebStorage, storage: localStorage });

if (!fs.existsSync('/test.txt')) {
        fs.writeFileSync('/test.txt', 'This will persist across reloads!');
}

const contents = fs.readFileSync('/test.txt', 'utf-8');
console.log(contents);
```

#### `XML`

The `XML` backend can be used to create a file system which lives in the DOM:

```html
<!-- ... -->
<fs />
<!-- ... -->
```

```js
import { configure, fs } from '@zenfs/core';
import { XML } from '@zenfs/dom';

await configureSingle({
        backend: XML,
        root: document.querySelector('fs'), // root is optional
});

fs.writeFileSync('/test.txt', 'This is in the DOM!');
```

If you choose to add the root element to the DOM by appending it, you will likel
y want to hide its contents (`display:none` works well).

The `root` option is not required. If you choose not to pass in a `root`, you ca
n always append it to the DOM later:

```js
import { configure, fs, mounts } from '@zenfs/core';
import { XML } from '@zenfs/dom';

await configureSingle({ backend: XML });

const { root } = mounts.get('/');

document.body.append(root);
```

This may disrupt use cases that involve saving the HTML file locally and loading
 it later, since a new element is created when configuring. In contrast, when us
ing an existing element and passing in a `root`, the existing element's contents
 will be preserved.

# SlipI-OS
its a web os, based on daedalos, but will use CheerpX as the Linux engine rather than slow v86

## Browser Application API

Applications are independent HTML files with assets referenced relative to their own HTML file. The desktop loads each app in an iframe. Launch flags are query parameters, so they do not change relative asset resolution:

```text
Applications/example/index.html?--is_windowed&--window_size=640x720
```

Use the desktop's Open app button or call `window.WebOS.openApp(url, options)`. App options support `title`, `icon`, `isWindowed`, `windowSize`, `width`, and `height`. The host also exposes `openWindow`, `openFileManager`, `getWindows`, `closeWindow`, `minimizeWindow`, `maximizeWindow`, `resizeWindow`, and async filesystem methods under `window.WebOS.filesystem`.

An app under `WebOS filesystem/Applications/<app>/` can load `../../app-api.js`. It exposes `window.WebOSApp.flags` (`isWindowed`, `windowSize`, and `windowId`) and `openApp`, `close`, `minimize`, `maximize`, `resize`, `setTitle`, and `setIcon`. App-to-host requests use `postMessage` and are accepted only from registered app iframes.

The API example is at `WebOS filesystem/Applications/api-example/index.html`. The Nuvola icon theme is extracted to `WebOS filesystem/Icons/nuvola/`; attribution and license notices are included with the theme.

## Xelite File Manager

Xelite is built into the desktop shell and is not an HTML file inside the browsable filesystem. It uses BrowserFS 1.4.3 with the IndexedDB backend (`slipi-os-browserfs`) for persistent browser storage. The initial root contains `Application files`, `Applications`, `Icons`, `Linux files`, `Public`, and `Trash`.

Use **Import folder** in Xelite to copy the workspace's `WebOS filesystem` folder into the browser filesystem. This requires an explicit folder selection because browser pages cannot directly mount or modify arbitrary workspace directories. Files created or edited in Xelite persist in IndexedDB; they do not write back to the workspace folder.

Xelite supports folder navigation, sorting, text-file editing, file/folder creation, rename, delete, upload, download, and folder import. The built-in manager itself is not stored in the user filesystem, so deleting files cannot remove Xelite.

11-
12-BrowserFS is highly extensible, and ships with many filesystem backends:
13-
14-* `XmlHttpRequest`: Downloads files on-demand from a webserver via `XMLHttpRe
quest`
15-* `LocalStorage`: Stores files in the browser's `localStorage`.
16-* `HTML5FS`: Stores files into the HTML5 `FileSystem` API
17:* `IndexedDB`: Stores files into the browser's `IndexedDB` object database.
18-* `Dropbox`: Stores files into the user's Dropbox account.
19-  * Note: You provide this filesystem with an authenticated [DropboxJS client
](https://github.com/dropbox/dropbox-js)
20-* `InMemory`: Stores files in-memory. Thus, it is a temporary file store that
 clears when the user navigates away.
21-* `ZipFS`: Read-only zip file-backed FS. Lazily decompresses files as you acc
ess them.
22-  * Supports DEFLATE out-of-the-box.
23-  * Have super old zip files? [The `browserfs-zipfs-extras` package](https://
github.com/jvilk/browserfs-zipfs-extras) adds support for EXPLODE, UNREDUCE, and
 UNSHRINK.
24-* `IsoFS`: Mount an .iso file into the file system.
25-  * Supports Microsoft Joliet and Rock Ridge extensions to the ISO9660 standa
rd.
26-* `WorkerFS`: Lets you mount the BrowserFS file system configured in the main
 thread in a WebWorker, or the other way around!
27-* `MountableFileSystem`: Lets you mount multiple file systems into a single d
irectory hierarchy, as in *nix-based OSes.
28-* `OverlayFS`: Mount a read-only file system as read-write by overlaying a wr
itable file system on top of it. Like Docker's overlayfs, it will only write cha
nged files to the writable file system.
29-* `AsyncMirror`: Use an asynchronous backend synchronously. Invaluable for Em
scripten; let your Emscripten applications write to larger file stores with no a
dditional effort!
30-  * Note: Loads the entire contents of the file system into a synchronous bac
kend during construction. Performs synchronous operations in-memory, and enqueue
s them to be mirrored onto the asynchronous backend.
31-* `FolderAdapter`: Wraps a file system, and scopes all interactions to a subf
older of that file system.
32-* `Emscripten`: Lets you mount Emscripten file systems inside BrowserFS.
33-
34-More backends can be defined by separate libraries, so long as they extend th
e `BaseFileSystem` class. Multiple backends can be active at once at different l
ocations in the directory hierarchy.

edits.text:
# SlipI-OS
its a web os, based on daedalos, but will use CheerpX as the Linux engine rather than slow v86

## Browser Application API

Applications are independent HTML files with assets referenced relative to their own HTML file. The desktop loads each app in an iframe. Launch flags are query parameters, so they do not change relative asset resolution:

```text
Applications/example/index.html?--is_windowed&--window_size=640x720
```

Use the desktop's Open app button or call `window.WebOS.openApp(url, options)`. App options support `title`, `icon`, `isWindowed`, `windowSize`, `width`, and `height`. The host also exposes `openWindow`, `openFileManager`, `getWindows`, `closeWindow`, `minimizeWindow`, `maximizeWindow`, `resizeWindow`, and async filesystem methods under `window.WebOS.filesystem`.

An app under `WebOS filesystem/Applications/<app>/` can load `../../app-api.js`. It exposes `window.WebOSApp.flags` (`isWindowed`, `windowSize`, and `windowId`) and `openApp`, `close`, `minimize`, `maximize`, `resize`, `setTitle`, and `setIcon`. App-to-host requests use `postMessage` and are accepted only from registered app iframes.

The API example is at `WebOS filesystem/Applications/api-example/index.html`. The Nuvola icon theme is extracted to `WebOS filesystem/Icons/nuvola/`; attribution and license notices are included with the theme.

## Xelite File Manager

Xelite is built into the desktop shell and is not an HTML file inside the browsable filesystem. It uses BrowserFS 1.4.3 with `AsyncMirror` and the IndexedDB backend (`slipi-os-browserfs`) for persistent browser storage. On first run, `filesystem-manifest.json` seeds the full `WebOS filesystem` tree into the BrowserFS root.

`Application files`, `Applications`, `Icons`, and `Linux files` are read-only system paths. `Public` and `Trash` are writable. **Import folder** copies selected folder contents into `Public`; file imports go to the current writable folder. This is a one-way seed/copy: browser pages cannot directly mount or modify the workspace directory. User changes persist in IndexedDB and do not write back to the workspace folder.

Xelite supports folder navigation, sorting, text-file editing, file/folder creation, rename, delete, upload, download, and folder import. The built-in manager itself is not stored in the user filesystem, so deleting files cannot remove Xelite.

edits.text:
# SlipI-OS
its a web os, based on daedalos, but will use CheerpX as the Linux engine rather than slow v86

## Browser Application API

Applications are independent HTML files with assets referenced relative to their own HTML file. The desktop loads each app in an iframe. Launch flags are query parameters, so they do not change relative asset resolution:

```text
Applications/example/index.html?--is_windowed&--window_size=640x720
```

Use the desktop's Open app button or call `window.WebOS.openApp(url, options)`. App options support `title`, `icon`, `isWindowed`, `windowSize`, `width`, and `height`. The host also exposes `openWindow`, `openFileManager`, `getWindows`, `closeWindow`, `minimizeWindow`, `maximizeWindow`, `resizeWindow`, and async filesystem methods under `window.WebOS.filesystem`.

An app under `WebOS filesystem/Applications/<app>/` can load `../../app-api.js`. It exposes `window.WebOSApp.flags` (`isWindowed`, `windowSize`, and `windowId`) and `openApp`, `close`, `minimize`, `maximize`, `resize`, `setTitle`, and `setIcon`. App-to-host requests use `postMessage` and are accepted only from registered app iframes.

The API example is at `WebOS filesystem/Applications/api-example/index.html`. The Nuvola icon theme is extracted to `WebOS filesystem/Icons/nuvola/`; attribution and license notices are included with the theme.

## Xelite File Manager

Xelite is built into the desktop shell and is not an HTML file inside the browsable filesystem. It uses BrowserFS 1.4.3 with `AsyncMirror` and the IndexedDB backend (`slipi-os-browserfs`) for persistent browser storage. On first run, `filesystem-manifest.json` seeds the application/system files into the BrowserFS root, excluding the Nuvola icon pack.

`Application files`, `Applications`, and `Linux files` are read-only system paths. The Nuvola icon pack remains a static UI asset outside the user filesystem; it is not seeded into BrowserFS. `Public` and `Trash` are writable. **Import folder** copies selected folder contents into `Public`; file imports go to the current writable folder. This is a one-way seed/copy: browser pages cannot directly mount or modify the workspace directory. User changes persist in IndexedDB and do not write back to the workspace folder.

Xelite supports folder navigation, sorting, text-file editing, file/folder creation, rename, delete, upload, download, and folder import. The built-in manager itself is not stored in the user filesystem, so deleting files cannot remove Xelite.

# SlipI-OS
its a web os, based on daedalos, but will use CheerpX as the Linux engine rather than slow v86

## Browser Application API

Applications are independent HTML files with assets referenced relative to their own HTML file. The desktop loads each app in an iframe. Launch flags are query parameters, so they do not change relative asset resolution:

```text
Applications/example/index.html?--is_windowed&--window_size=640x720
```

Use the desktop's Open app button or call `window.WebOS.openApp(url, options)`. App options support `title`, `icon`, `isWindowed`, `windowSize`, `width`, and `height`. The host also exposes `openWindow`, `openFileManager`, `getWindows`, `closeWindow`, `minimizeWindow`, `maximizeWindow`, `resizeWindow`, and async filesystem methods under `window.WebOS.filesystem`.

An app under `WebOS filesystem/Applications/<app>/` can load `../../app-api.js`. It exposes `window.WebOSApp.flags` (`isWindowed`, `windowSize`, and `windowId`) and `openApp`, `close`, `minimize`, `maximize`, `resize`, `setTitle`, and `setIcon`. App-to-host requests use `postMessage` and are accepted only from registered app iframes.

The API example is at `WebOS filesystem/Applications/api-example/index.html`. The Nuvola icon theme is extracted to `WebOS filesystem/Icons/nuvola/`; attribution and license notices are included with the theme.

## Xelite File Manager

Xelite is built into the desktop shell and is not an HTML file inside the browsable filesystem. It uses BrowserFS 1.4.3 with `AsyncMirror` and the IndexedDB backend (`slipi-os-browserfs`) for persistent browser storage. On first run, `filesystem-manifest.json` seeds the application/system files into the BrowserFS root, excluding the Nuvola icon pack.

`Application files`, `Applications`, and `Linux files` are read-only system paths. The Nuvola icon pack remains a static UI asset outside the user filesystem; it is not seeded into BrowserFS. `Public` and `Trash` are writable. **Import folder** copies selected folder contents into `Public`; file imports go to the current writable folder. This is a one-way seed/copy: browser pages cannot directly mount or modify the workspace directory. User changes persist in IndexedDB and do not write back to the workspace folder.

Xelite supports folder navigation, sorting, text-file editing, file/folder creation, rename, delete, upload, download, and folder import. The built-in manager itself is not stored in the user filesystem, so deleting files cannot remove Xelite.

## Application Dock

children.text: Xelite is built into the desktop shell and is not an HTML file inside the browsable filesystem. It uses BrowserFS 1.4.3 with `AsyncMirror` and the IndexedDB backend (`slipi-os-browserfs`) for persistent browser storage. On first run, `filesystem-manifest.json` seeds the application/system files into the BrowserFS root, excluding the Nuvola icon pack.

`Application files`, `Applications`, and `Linux files` are read-only system paths. The Nuvola icon pack remains a static UI asset outside the user filesystem; it is not seeded into BrowserFS. `Public` and `Trash` are writable. **Import folder** copies selected folder contents into `Public`; file imports go to the current writable folder. This is a one-way seed/copy: browser pages cannot directly mount or modify the workspace directory. User changes persist in IndexedDB and do not write back to the workspace folder.

Xelite supports folder navigation, sorting, text-file editing, file/folder creation, rename, delete, upload, download, and folder import. The built-in manager itself is not stored in the user filesystem, so deleting files cannot remove Xelite.

The style block below uses this class to hide [data-filter-section] (the filter bar + card grid on showcase/blog pages). ProductFilter.svelte initialises its filter state synchronously from the URL (outside onMount), so its first rendered output already shows the correct filtered state. A $effect removes "filtering-pending" after that first render, so the section fades in cleanly. This is the same no-FOUC pattern used for dark-mode theme scripts. --> Search / 👽 No results If you have a question, please ask it in our Discord server. Join the Discord server Docs Blog Demos Licensing Close navigation Overview Quickstart Guides Files and filesystems Networking Custom disk images Input and output Basic server setup Tutorials Full OS CheerpX with NPM Simple Executable Reference CheerpX.Linux create run setConsole setActivateConsole setCustomConsole setKmsCanvas event callbacks CheerpX.DataDevice create writeFile CheerpX.HttpBytesDevice create CheerpX.IDBDevice create readFileAsBlob reset CheerpX.OverlayDevice create CheerpX.WebDevice create Frequently Asked Questions Licensing Open navigation menu Custom disk images How to create custom ext2 images to use as a filesystem for CheerpX This guide shows how to setup an OCI image and build it into an ext2 disk image that CheerpX can use as its filesystem. An OCI image is a packaged, ready-to-run snapshot of a filesystem (everything an app needs to run). Here we build one, then convert its filesystem into an ext2 disk image for CheerpX. New to images? See Docker’s What is an image? . Prerequisites: a Linux host with buildah and mkfs.ext2 installed. 1. Creating our OCI image 1.1 Create a Dockerfile First, create your Dockerfile to define the environment. Here’s an example of a Dockerfile that installs the curl command: FROM --platform=linux/i386 docker.io/i386/debian:buster ARG DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive # Point APT to the archived mirrors (Buster is EOL) RUN echo "deb [trusted=yes] http://archive.debian.org/debian buster main contrib non-free" \ > /etc/apt/sources.list && \ echo "deb [trusted=yes] http://archive.debian.org/debian-security buster/updates main" \ >> /etc/apt/sources.list RUN apt-get update && apt-get -y upgrade && apt-get -y install curl /etc/apt/sources.list && \ echo "deb [trusted=yes] http://archive.debian.org/debian-security buster/updates main" \ >> /etc/apt/sources.listRUN apt-get update && apt-get -y upgrade && apt-get -y install curl"> Note The base image’s architecture must be 32-bit x86 (for example, i386 or i686). 1.2 Creating our image Once the Dockerfile is ready, use buildah to create an OCI image. Terminal window buildah build -f Dockerfile --dns=none --platform linux/i386 -t cheerpximage 1.3 Create a container from the OCI Image Now that we have our image, we can build our container Terminal window buildah from --name cheerpxcontainer cheerpximage 2 Building our ext2 image With the container created, we can now use its filesystem to build the actual ext2 disk image that will be used by CheerpX. 2.1 Enter a user namespace We will use buildah unshare to enter ‘rootless mode’. This way we can mount the container safely without requiring actual root privileges. Terminal window buildah unshare 2.2 Mount the container filesystem Now we can safely mount the filesystem to our host machine to build our image from it. Be sure to save the outputted path for the next 2 steps! Terminal window buildah mount cheerpxcontainer Seeing a subuid/subgid or “potentially insufficient UIDs or GIDs” error here? See the optional /etc/subgid step at the end of this guide. 2.3 Check filesystem size We’ll quickly check the size of our mounted filesystem so we know how much size we should allocate for the ext2 image Terminal window du -sh " your/path/to/mountpoint " Reserve (a little) extra space We recommend allocating a bit more than the size of the filesystem to prevent “out of space” errors. (Files will get stored in the browser, but the image still needs to see some space available.) Though do please also note that the max image size for CheerpX is 2GB 2.4 Build the image Pass the mount path outputted by buildah mount to mkfs.ext2 to finally build our disk image! Terminal window mkfs.ext2 -b 4096 -d your/path/to/mountpoint cheerpXImage.ext2 600M 2.5 Clean up Now that we have our ext2 disk image, we can go ahead and clean up everything else. Terminal window buildah umount cheerpxcontainer buildah rm cheerpxcontainer exit buildah rmi cheerpximage Conclusion Congratulations! You have successfully created a custom ext2 image that can be used as a filesystem for CheerpX. This image is now ready to be loaded into your CheerpX environment for further testing and deployment. If you’d like to see more details on how to implement the custom ext2 image with CheerpX, please refer to the Full OS tutorial. Optional: edit /etc/subgid (for the host user) The /etc/subgid file defines the ranges of subordinate group IDs allocated to specific user accounts on the host for managing user namespaces in containers. This step is optional and not necessary for most use cases — most systems set this up automatically. You only need it if mounting the container (step 2.2) fails with a subuid / subgid or UID/GID mapping error. After editing the file, re-run the build from step 2.1. 1. Identify your host user Run the following command to determine the host user running container commands: Terminal window whoami 2. Check /etc/subgid for your user Open /etc/subgid and look for an entry matching your user: Terminal window sudo nano /etc/subgid The file should contain lines in the format: <username>:<start_id>:<count> : : "> For example, for the user johndoe : johndoe:100000:65536 3. Modify the file If you need to change the subgid range for the host user, modify the start_id and/or count as needed. For example, if you want to assign a new range starting at 200000 with a count of 65536, you would change it to: johndoe:200000:65536 For more information about subgid , refer to the subgid documentation . and build it into an ext2 disk image that CheerpX can use as its filesystem. An
OCI image is a packaged, ready-to-run snapshot of a filesystem (everything an ap
p needs to run). Here we build one, then convert its filesystem into an ext2 dis

es: a Linux host with buildah and mkfs.ext2 installed. 1. Creating our OCI image

orm=linux/i386 docker.io/i386/debian:buster ARG DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive #

uster/updates main" \ >> /etc/apt/sources.list RUN apt-get update && apt-get -y

eated, we can now use its filesystem to build the actual ext2 disk image that wi

ring actual root privileges. Terminal window buildah unshare 2.2 Mount the conta
iner filesystem Now we can safely mount the filesystem to our host machine to bu
ild our image from it. Be sure to save the outputted path for the next 2 steps!
Terminal window buildah mount cheerpxcontainer Seeing a subuid/subgid or “potent
